summary:
Amazonas stands under Peru's national framework: the department has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern, and none of the sources covering this territory contain Amazonas-specific content. What a trans visitor faces in Amazonas is the national statute book, national policing and national monitoring data.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities. On 20 February 2025 the Comision de Mujer y Familia of the Congress approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex. The exceptions are narrow: custody, and cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities. Venues would also be obliged not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The text still required plenary backing at that date, and the reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho argued that the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes, whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis of 15 April 2025 by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The restriction reaches private as well as public life. INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, which grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI. Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so the document a visitor carries will generally carry the sex marker assigned at birth. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women, and the killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

One case illustrates the pattern of violence and the delay of remedy. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots; Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, had been shot days earlier. Two killers were arrested in March 2023. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. IDEHPUCP found the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are also constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

The 2017 repeal left it one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime provisions, which affects how a visitor's case would be classified if reported.

Recorded killings of trans people in Peru are concentrated in urban centres such as Lima, and the state's crime-registration systems do not record sexual orientation or gender identity, so the national figures understate incidence everywhere, including in Amazonas.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights' Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 binds regional states to recognise gender identity as protected personal autonomy, and the December 2025 Azul Rojas Marín judgment shows the Inter-American mechanism can produce a remedy where domestic proceedings fail, though after decades.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory contains Amazonas-specific content: there is no record of a departmental ordinance, a local police practice, a local court decision or a recorded incident of violence against a trans person in Amazonas. The absence of such material is unresolved rather than evidence that no such law or incident exists.

How Article 5.1 is enforced on the ground in Amazonas is not sourced. The DNI-check mechanism described by Gianna Camacho is an argument about how enforcement would work, not a documented practice in this department.

The 54 killings and 170 violation cases are national totals for 2020-2023 with no departmental breakdown available, and the source states the recorded figures are only a sub-registry; no Amazonas figure can be verified from this inventory.

Whether the July 2025 Lima constitutional court ruling against an anti-equality decree affects the April 2025 bathroom provision is not stated in the sources and remains unresolved.
